content: Crops cultivated on contaminated land and animals grazing on such land can accumulate lead, which subsequently becomes a source of lead exposure for consumers. Similarly, hunted game shot with lead ammunition poses a risk of lead exposure to individuals who consume this meat. Lead from ammunition can contaminate the animal's flesh, and embedded lead shot may be ingested, retained in the gastrointestinal tract, and absorbed. Outbreaks of lead poisoning have been linked to flour ground with millstones containing lead components. Spices may be intentionally adulterated with lead compounds or contaminated through other means. Traditional medicines may contain lead either as an intended ingredient or as a contaminant, leading to numerous cases of poisoning in both children and adults. These medicines are often used for conditions such as gastrointestinal complaints, skin conditions, infertility, erectile dysfunction, epilepsy, and diabetes, or as tonics or aphrodisiacs. The use of traditional cosmetics containing lead, such as surma, kohl, and sindoor, has also caused toxic effects, particularly in children. Children can be exposed to lead by mouthing toys painted with lead-based paint, brass keys, or by accidentally swallowing lead objects like fishing weights, curtain weights, or lead jewelry. Adults may also ingest lead foreign bodies, either intentionally or accidentally, such as lead shot in hunted game. Pregnant women ingesting lead-glazed pottery can experience maternal and fetal lead poisoning. Lead exposure is a significant occupational hazard, as it is the most widely used non-ferrous metal. The primary routes of lead exposure are ingestion and inhalation. Acute lead poisoning can occur after ingesting toxic amounts of lead salts, such as lead acetate or lead tetroxide. However, most cases of oral lead poisoning result from chronic ingestion of small amounts of lead-containing materials, such as contaminated dust, soil, lead paint flakes, contaminated food, or traditional medicines. Young children are particularly vulnerable due to their behaviors, such as playing on the ground and frequent hand-to-mouth contact. Inhalation of lead fumes or particles is a major occupational exposure route and can also occur in homes with airborne lead-contaminated dust, such as during paint stripping. Dermal exposure to lead is minimal for inorganic lead but more significant for organic lead compounds. Injection of lead compounds has been occasionally reported. Once absorbed, lead is initially bound to erythrocytes in the blood and distributed to soft tissues and bone. Blood and soft tissues represent the active pool, while bone serves as the storage pool. Lead accumulates in bone over a lifetime, up to the age of 50–60 years, after which it decreases due to age-related changes in diet, hormonal levels, and metabolism. During pregnancy, blood lead levels increase due to the resorption of maternal bone to meet the calcium needs of the developing fetal skeleton. Lead can cross the placenta, and maternal and fetal blood lead concentrations are similar. Lead is also present in breast milk, though no cases of lead poisoning from breast milk alone have been identified. Lead exerts toxic effects on all parts of the nervous system, with many effects being irreversible. Severe lead poisoning can result in life-threatening encephalopathy, particularly in young children. Chronic lead exposure may cause subtle neurological and cognitive deficits in both children and adults, including reduced cognition, behavioral changes, and impaired learning and memory. Lead exposure is also associated with cardiovascular effects, such as increased blood pressure and a higher risk of cardiovascular disease.
